attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter post, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: 'Will continue until' is firm language. 'Likely' only describes what people will come to realise, so it does not hedge the forecast itself. The reward-environment scope and the open-source-then-abandonment sequence are both kept.

contract.note: Reading this as a broad trend rather than literal unanimity is a fair, ordinary plain reading. There is no deadline, and the contract rightly says continued spending cannot disprove it. The result depends on how 'everybody' and 'open source' are read.

evidence.note: Business Insider report dated before the post: Accenture, Meta and Google tie AI use to performance reviews. This bears on the reward condition, not the forecast outcome.
ETR survey fielded June–July 2026: enterprises keep funding AI overruns. This matches the starting state but says nothing about later migration or abandonment.

reviews.rationale: This is an undated forecast that enterprise spending continues until a cost realisation leads to open-source migration and then abandonment. The packet only shows the condition (rewards for adoption) and continued funding. No evidence shows the migration and abandonment sequence, and no conclusive event has occurred. It stays unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in the post.

semantics.note: The draft broadens 'these companies' (Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta in context) to 'AI labs'. The contract restores the named labs. Both the claimed inability and the causal link are captured.

contract.note: Requiring evidence of both the inability and its causal role in benchmark-focused development is fair to the speaker's words. Motives are hard to observe, but the criteria do not stretch the claim.

evidence.note: Anthropic disclosure from July 2026 on robotics tasks: shows both limits and gains in a narrow domain. It does not address why labs focus on benchmarks.
Anthropic reward-hacking study from November 2025, before the target period: reports training failures and some mitigations. It neither establishes nor refutes the claimed causal link.

reviews.rationale: Neither item addresses why the named labs focus on benchmarks, or whether they broadly cannot train models for reliable task performance. Both are narrow company disclosures. The causal claim is neither shown nor refuted.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in the post.

semantics.note: 'So confident AI gets cut' is high-confidence firm language, so it is a scored forecast. The stated reasons (volatile costs, higher than anything else) are premises. Phrasing the claim as 'Zitron is confident' is awkward, but the commitment is the same.

contract.note: Reading 'AI gets cut' as broad material cuts to spending is an ordinary plain reading, though 'cuts to projects' is another possible reading. The contract keeps the 'anything else in an organization' comparison as an unchecked premise. There is no deadline.

evidence.note: Cloudera-commissioned survey released 26 October 2026, before the evaluation date: 89% limited or redesigned use cases and 45% moved workloads over costs. That is a company disclosure and is not a cut in total spending.
ETR survey dated before the post: only 17% of over-budget firms scale back. This is baseline only and does not measure later cuts.

reviews.rationale: This is an undated, confident forecast that enterprise AI spending gets cut because of high and volatile costs. The Cloudera survey shows cost-driven redesign and workload moves, but not a broad, realised fall in spending, and it is a vendor disclosure. No conclusive event meets the early-resolution rule, so it stays unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in the post.

semantics.note: Pulls out the reliability assertion and leaves aside the marketing and motive parts of the sentence. That is acceptable, because the extracted part is a definite assertion Zitron made. The 'even in things they mostly get right' scope is kept.

contract.note: The plain reading (models that usually succeed still sometimes fail) is fair and ordinary. Choosing April–June 2026 as the period is reasonable, since Zitron gave none.

evidence.note: Princeton paper (ICML 2026) released 2 June 2026, within the target period: five runs per task across 15 models. Agents that can solve a task often fail to do so consistently.
Microsoft Research blog of 15 May 2026: a stress test finds sparse errors, but the authors warn against generalising. Company disclosure; it does not show error-free performance.

reviews.rationale: The independent, peer-reviewed June 2026 evaluation finds low outcome consistency across all 15 models: tasks they can solve still fail on repeat runs. That matches the support condition. The Microsoft caveats limit wider inferences about usefulness, but they show no dependable error-free performance.
